verdicts.trueWording: "writers of history often seek the dramatic over the truth" (Sailing 1)
verdicts.note: Byline on page: "by Jillian Hatch, 2005" (BrightWeavings, Student Papers). Page: "At the end of the very first paragraph on the very first page of the first book in the Sarantine Mosaic, Kay's narrator claims that, 'writers of history often seek the dramatic over the truth' (Sailing 1)." Quote verbatim; every limb (first page, narrator, Mosaic) supported. Raw HTML fetched with a browser UA and stripped locally; no summarizer.

verdicts.trueWording: focused on both the affairs of leaders as well as the 'common' man
verdicts.note: Page: "Kay's narrative is focused on both the affairs of leaders as well as those of the 'common' man. This lack of a traditional 'historical' emphasis is demonstrative of Carl Schorske's claim..." Quote verbatim; the 'unlike traditional history' limb is carried by the next sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: only supernatural the societies believed; shown inside-out; setting renders beliefs true
verdicts.note: Cawsey's introduction (p.310): "the rest of Kay's works follow this general rule: they only contain elements of the supernatural that the original societies would have believed or at least half-believed"; "show the beliefs and assumptions of a time period from the inside-out"; "Kay says in the Tolkien lecture that the setting 'renders these beliefs as true.'" Two minor page qualifiers the claim drops but does not contradict: "or at least half-believed", and Ysabel (2007) is named as the exception. The quoted phrase is Kay's, from the Tolkien lecture, as reported in Cawsey's introduction. PDF fetched directly and text-extracted with pypdf.

verdicts.trueWording: Kay adapts Bagehot; leaves workings of magic unexplained; characters would not analyze beliefs
verdicts.note: Page (p.310): "He also quoted Walter Bagehot, who said that 'we must not let daylight in upon magic.' ... Kay adapts the saying to explain why he leaves the exact details of the workings of magic unexplained in his works" and "The characters would not question or analyze their beliefs, and so neither do the readers." Quote verbatim; all limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: death of the emperor far off means far less than the hired hand's broken leg
verdicts.note: Kay's answer (p.315): "I am profoundly interested in bringing 'great events' down to the personal level, so yes, this idea of the personal runs through much of my fiction. The death of the emperor far off means far less to a farmer than the broken leg of his hired hand at harvest time (Yeats wrote about this)..." Quote verbatim; page says "much of my fiction", claim says "his fiction" — same substance.

verdicts.trueWording: benefits from a major strand in the last generation or so of historians
verdicts.note: Kay (p.317): "I have, in recent years and books, become even more engaged by this idea of giving value to lives that often go unrecorded. This, by the way, links up and benefits from a major strand in the last generation or so of historians, who have—sometimes brilliantly—done exactly this, and who have thus provided me with superb research materials and inspiration!" Quote verbatim (the PDF breaks it as "giv-\ning" across a line). Flag for transparency: the page never uses the term "social history"; "recent social history" is the claim's own label for that strand of historians, an accurate gloss rather than page wording.

verdicts.trueWording: a drive towards complexity, I think—even towards celebrating it
verdicts.note: Kay (p.316): "I also have a drive towards complexity, I think—even towards celebrating it. That can, as a side note, cut hard against the cultural tendencies of our own day, but I don't mind that either." Quote verbatim (PDF hyphenates "to-\nwards"); the 'against the cultural tendencies of the day' limb is the next sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: absence of specific time and place; readers wanting to be 'educated' find it frustrating
verdicts.note: Kay (pp.313-314): "I think the absence of a specific time and place can cause a reader to be able to see a story as not tied to, not solely about, a particular time and place." The cost limb is answered at the next question ("Is there anything lost in that universalization?"): "you can gain and lose readers! There will always be those who want a novel to 'educate' them about ... the fall of Muslim Spain. These readers can find this shift into an invented setting frustrating." Quote verbatim; all limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Frazer, Graves, Campbell, Mabinogion, Malory, Poetic Edda; "so much steeped in myth"
verdicts.note: Kay (p.312), answering what lies behind The Fionavar Tapestry: "James George Frazer's The Golden Bough (1890), Robert Graves' The White Goddess (1948), Joseph Campbell, The Mabinogion (1840), Thomas Malory, The Poetic Edda. I was so much steeped in myth, legend, and folklore at that time. The trilogy is infused with it." Quote verbatim (PDF hyphenates "folk-\nlore"); the six names and the first-trilogy framing all check out.

verdicts.trueWording: detaches the tale from a narrow context; eroding of prejudices; not only Spain
verdicts.note: Kay, 'Home and Away' (Wayback id_ capture, raw HTML): "It detaches the tale from a narrow context, permits a stripping away, or at least an eroding of prejudices and assumptions. ... It cannot be read as being only about something that happened, say, seven hundred years ago in Spain." Quote verbatim; all three limbs supported.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that treating the past as fantasy acknowledges the IMPOSSIBILITY of recovering past world-views — the page says it acknowledges "the sort of difficulties James was referring to", and Kay expressly rejects James's impossibility thesis ("I don't agree, but I see the point")
verdicts.trueWording: acknowledges the sort of difficulties James referred to — while disagreeing
verdicts.note: Quote "a way of being honest about limitations" is verbatim on the page, and the Henry James framing is real: "It was Henry James who argued that historical fiction was, in fact, impossible ... getting to 'the real thing' with regard to the world views of people in the past simply could not be done." But Kay's own sentence is "I don't agree, but I see the point, and it strikes me forcibly that by treating the past through the form of a fantasy, one acknowledges the sort of difficulties James was referring to, while still probing and revealing motifs of the past." Difficulties acknowledged, impossibility disputed — so the claim's 'impossibility' limb overstates the source.

verdicts.trueWording: inventing a man based on Rodrigo Diaz but clearly not him; declaring I did not know
verdicts.note: Page: "El Cid was a real person who became - for good or ill - the symbol of a society ... by inventing the setting and inventing a man based on Rodrigo Diaz but clearly not him, I might also be demonstrating a measure of appropriate distance. I would be declaring, without pretense, that I did not know what the real man was like nine hundred years ago ... we are all guessing." Quote verbatim; the page names Rodrigo Diaz and identifies him as El Cid in the same passage, so the El Cid limb holds.

verdicts.trueWording: Douglas Barbour described a fantasy he admired as 'The kind of escape that brings you home'
verdicts.note: Page: "Many years ago, the poet and critic, Douglas Barbour, described a fantasy he admired as, 'The kind of escape that brings you home.' I realized, reading these words, that this was how I'd always seen the potential of the genre. For me, that is what fantasy can do and be if we allow it." Quote verbatim; 'adopts ... for what fantasy can do' is exactly the following two sentences.

verdicts.trueWording: shape language and a form of telling the tale (using elements from the sagas)
verdicts.note: Eckford interview (BrightWeavings reprint of Historical Novels Review, Nov '04; interviewer named on page). The passage is explicitly about The Last Light of the Sun: "In The Last Light of the Sun ... This book is completely different from Kay's earlier works in terms of setting. His reasons for the change reveal much about his method:" then Kay: "the three previous novels had all been about exceptionally sophisticated, even decadent cultures ... a setting and peoples where that kind of urbane civilization wasn't even a dream yet ... I wanted to see if I could shape language and a form of telling the tale (using elements from the sagas) that would show that difference." Quote verbatim; all limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: reveal and showcase character within and through action scenes; "I doubt anyone's ever been better"
verdicts.note: Kay, in the influences passage: "Dunnett, along with Mary Renault, is my own nomination for the preeminent historical fiction writer of our time. In Lady Dunnett's case, I remain deeply admiring of her ability to reveal and showcase character within and through action scenes. I doubt anyone's ever been better." Quote verbatim; 'unmatched' = "I doubt anyone's ever been better", and the 'model' limb sits inside the interviewer's frame "the writers and experiences that have influenced Guy over the years". Minor: the page writes "Dunnett"/"Lady Dunnett" and never the first name "Dorothy" (2 occurrences of the surname, no 'Dorothy' on the page); the identification is unambiguous from context.
